definition: A distributional–relational database, or word-vector database, is a database management system (DBMS) that uses distributional word-vector representations to enrich the semantics of structured data.
details: As distributional word-vectors can be built automatically from large-scale corpora, this enrichment supports the construction of databases which can embed large-scale commonsense background knowledge into their operations. Distributional-Relational models can be applied to the construction of schema-agnostic databases (databases in which users can query the data without being aware of its schema), semantic search, schema-integration and inductive and abductive reasoning as well as different applications in which a semantically flexible knowledge representation model is needed. The main advantage of distributional–relational models over purely logical or semantic web models is the fact that the core semantic associations can be automatically captured from corpora, in contrast to the definition of manually curated ontologies and rule knowledge bases.

explainer.lead: A distributional–relational database combines structured data with word vectors learned from large text collections, giving database operations a flexible sense of word meaning. This can support commonsense background knowledge and semantic queries without relying entirely on hand-built ontologies and rules.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a filing cabinet that not only stores facts, but also knows from reading lots of text that some words are related. That can help it find useful information even when your question uses different words or you do not know how the cabinet is organised.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer can use this approach for schema-agnostic querying, semantic search, schema integration, or reasoning applications that need flexible semantics. Distributional vectors built automatically from large corpora supply the core semantic associations, reducing dependence on manually curated ontologies and rule knowledge bases.
tiers.paperLevel: A distributional–relational database is a DBMS that enriches structured data with distributional word-vector representations. Its distinguishing feature is that core semantic associations can be captured automatically from corpora, rather than being defined only through logical models, semantic-web ontologies, or rule bases.

explainer.example: Suppose a structured table contains a description using the word “cat,” while a user searches for a pet without knowing the table’s schema. Distributional associations learned from text can help connect the query with that description, without requiring someone to hand-write every relevant semantic rule.

explainer.intuition: A relational database stores structured facts, while distributional word vectors add associations between meanings learned from text. Together, they let the database handle meaning more flexibly than structure and hand-written rules alone.
howItWorks: Build distributional word vectors automatically from large-scale corpora.
Use those vectors to enrich the semantics of structured data.
Apply the enriched representation to queries, search, integration, or reasoning.
Use corpus-derived associations instead of relying solely on curated ontologies and rules.
explainer.whyItMatters: It offers a way to embed large-scale commonsense background knowledge into database operations automatically. This is useful when applications need semantically flexible knowledge representation rather than a rigid schema alone.
misconceptions: It is a DBMS approach, not simply a collection of word vectors.
It does not require users to know the schema in schema-agnostic applications.
Its core associations are learned from corpora, not manually curated.
It is not limited to semantic search; integration and reasoning are also applications.
